summary:
Ecuador's 2008 Constitution provides an explicit non-discrimination foundation for LGBTI people. Article 11 binds the state to respect differences of ethnicity, nationality, social and generational standing and gender, and extends expressly to sexual orientation and identity, within a secular, multinational state. The 1998 Constitution made Ecuador the first country in the Americas to bar discrimination based on sexual orientation.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1997, when Constitutional Tribunal Case No. 111-97-TC struck Article 516 of the Penal Code. The age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2019.

Legal gender recognition has been available since 2016. The 2016 Gender Identity Law permits a change of legal gender and birth name on identity documents solely by self-determination, without surgery or medical procedure. The National Assembly's 12 December 2023 reforms to the Organic Law on Identity Management and Civil Data were regulated by a decree issued by President Daniel Noboa on 11 June 2024, which streamlines the civil-registry procedure for changing a sex or gender marker and is the operative route for recognition. Outright's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, states that legal gender recognition is not available to people under 18.

Constitutional Court rulings have nevertheless extended document changes to trans adolescents. Rulings in 2024 and 2025 allowed trans adolescents to change name and sex on official records and publicly rebuked the National Assembly for stalling implementation of trans-rights legislation; an April 2026 report describes the adolescent ruling as opening a path for others seeking legal recognition.

Conversion practices amounting to torture are criminalised. Article 151 of the Penal Code, adopted in 2014, treats conversion therapy as equivalent to torture and carries 7 to 10 years' imprisonment. Enforcement does not match the statute: as of 2023, hundreds of clinics were still promoting the practice.

Violence against LGBTQ Ecuadorians was reported to be increasing amid the country's internal armed conflict in January 2024. A 2011 human rights report recorded discrimination based on sexual orientation among societal problems, found that gay, lesbian and transgender people suffered discrimination from public and private bodies, and recorded LGBT group claims that police and prosecutors did not thoroughly investigate deaths of LGBT individuals. The same report found that the right of LGBT community members to equal access to formal education was frequently violated.

Detention carries acute risk for trans visitors and residents alike. Ecuador's prisons are almost always male, and trans women are held in male pavilions and placed by birth sex or legal sex rather than by gender identity, with a separate pavilion for vulnerable populations applied unevenly. Silueta X documents gender-identity discrimination, unsafe placement, sexual violence, forced suppression of gender expression and barriers to health care. Trans woman Helen Maldonado died during the November 2021 massacre at Penitenciaria del Litoral while held in a male prison space. A 2022 complaint alleged cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment of trans women in Lago Agrio; 2024 allegations included forced head-shaving, beatings and violence targeting breast and body implants; and the 2026 death in state custody of a 23-year-old trans woman at the El Encuentro maximum-security prison drew calls for an independent investigation. An international investigation documented rapes and torture reported to be directed at prisoners' gender identity, and a Venezuelan trans woman detained in August 2023 at Penitenciaria del Litoral was sent to a male pavilion rather than the vulnerable-populations pavilion, where she received no medical examinations or HIV treatment.
tangentialFactors:
Family recognition runs against the current of the identity framework. Article 68 of the Constitution limits adoption to different-sex couples, and on 14 August 2026 new adoption legislation passed 118-0 explicitly prohibiting single and same-sex couples from adopting. The 2018 Constitutional Court decision ordering the Civil Registry to register the daughter of a same-sex couple, Helen Bicknell and Nicola Rothon, established recognition of the child Satya Amani Bicknell Rothon and was described by lawyer Jose Luis Guerra as a precedent ordering state recognition of same-sex families; it did not open adoption.

Societal attitudes are markedly more conservative than the statutory framework. A macho culture in which homosexuality tends to be viewed negatively persists, and clinics have confined young people against their will, including the daughter of parents who unsuccessfully sought her release. Pride marches have nonetheless been authorised in all major cities with police protection and official participation; a 2011 Guayaquil march included a vice prefect, a city councillor and a National Assembly member, attendance reached about 20,000 in Guayaquil in 2017 and over 18,000 in Quito in 2018, and monuments and the Presidential House were lit in rainbow colours in 2017. Presidential candidate Nelson Zavala was fined over $3,000 and barred from office for a year in 2013 for calling gay people sinners and immoral. Diane Marie Rodríguez Zambrano became the first openly transgender candidate in 2013 and the first transgender lawmaker in 2017.

The 2011 report's evidence is now dated, and it records problems that predate both the 2016 Gender Identity Law and the 2024 regulation; it is indicative of institutional pattern rather than of the present enforcement climate.
localsOnly:
Ecuadorians change a sex or gender marker once, at the civil registry, under the December 2023 reforms as regulated on 11 June 2024; the procedure does not require surgery. The 2016 Gender Identity Law governs change of legal gender and birth name on national identity documents by self-determination.

Resident trans people in custody are the population most exposed. Silueta X's PrisioTrans programme, covering 2011 to 2026, records that trans women are held in male spaces across a prison system that is almost universally male. The last prison census counted 73 trans women across all Ecuadorian prisons, while Fundacion Vivir Libre states the true number is far higher. The programme does not press a single placement rule; it advocates individualised housing decisions under Inter-American standards that weigh gender identity, safety, the detainee's own assessment and informed consent, and cites a July 2016 government decision to develop protocols for LGBT people deprived of liberty. Protective placement in a vulnerable-populations pavilion exists but is used unevenly.

Residents also face the adoption prohibition of Article 68 and the August 2026 statute, restrictions on equal access to education recorded in the 2011 report, and continued operation of conversion clinics despite Article 151.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses entry, visa screening or border and airport document checks, so the treatment of a visitor whose passport marker differs from presentation is unresolved here.

Whether the 2016 recognition procedure and the 2024 regulation extend to passports and other externally issued documents, rather than to national identity documents and the civil registry, is not sourced.

No source identifies a hate-crime statute that names gender identity specifically; the 2011 report's findings on investigation of LGBT deaths are dated and no later official evaluation of investigative practice is available.

Outcomes of the investigations called for after the 2024 and 2026 prison allegations, and of the case concerning forced head-shaving and beatings, are not sourced. The count of conversion clinics still operating as of 2023 is not corroborated by a second source, and no enforcement data on Article 151 convictions is available.

Statistics quantifying violence against transgender people specifically, as distinct from LGBTQ people generally, are not sourced.
